name: Andrew Jackson
summary: Jackson governed as a champion of white male farmers and laborers against what he called the moneyed few, rejecting a national bank, protective tariffs, federal internal improvements and constructive readings of federal power. He insisted on the permanence of the Union, rejecting nullification and secession by force, and drove Indian removal while defending slaveholders' rights against abolitionist agitation.

property-fundamental.rationale: Said the Constitution had secured the rights of property and objected to measures that disturb property rights of the slaveholding states; yet his removal policy overrode Native land claims, so the answer is mixed.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Sought to end the Bank of the United States as a privileged corporation and urged the people to check state-chartered banks and corporations with exclusive privileges (Bank veto, Farewell).

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Vetoed the Bank's recharter and fought paper money in favour of gold and silver, but said a bank of the United States could be convenient and useful if purely national and constitutional; points both ways.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Objected to the Bank's power over the money supply outside popular control, asserted the President's authority over deposit of public funds, and argued the Bank was an agent of the executive branch.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: In the Farewell he said tariffs fell oppressively on farmers and labourers and that manufacturers sought high duties for gain; his first message said duties should place domestic goods in fair competition, with a possible exception for war necessities. He signed the reduced 1832 tariff.

free-trade.rationale: Regretted that the complicated restrictions on trade could not be abolished by common consent and let commerce flow where enterprise directs it, while saying the US must adapt to other nations' restrictions.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Pledged strict economy, paid off the national debt, said a long-lasting debt was incompatible with independence and that profuse spending breeds profligacy. Stimulus itself was not discussed.

no-business-privileges.rationale: In the Bank veto he took a stand against all new grants of monopolies and exclusive privileges that make the rich richer; the Farewell repeats it.

ban-cartels.rationale: His Bank war aimed to end a chartered monopoly and the concentration of the money power; he did not address cartels or competition law as such.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Farewell warned that the organised money power would have moved the government from the many to the few and that concentrated moneyed corporations endanger free institutions.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Condemned a currency system that fosters the desire to amass wealth without labour and said farmers, mechanics and labourers prosper by industry and economy; objected to gratuities to stockholders.

taxation-theft.rationale: Accepted taxation for constitutional purposes (tariff and land revenue), calling only excess or unnecessary taxation an abuse and oppressive.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Proposed reducing duties on tea and coffee first, as articles of necessity used by all classes, and urged reducing taxes to what the government needs.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Praised the farmers, mechanics and planters who hold the national wealth in moderate amounts among millions, and fought concentrated corporate power.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Argued in the Bank veto that foreign ownership of the Bank's stock endangered American liberty and independence and that any such bank should be wholly American.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Rejected federal subscriptions to private companies, the Maysville road and protective tariffs aimed at favoured industries as unconstitutional or dangerous.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Insisted on strictly limited, enumerated federal powers and rejected internal improvements, but his government still ran a post office, army, navy and Indian affairs beyond bare defence and justice.

decide-locally.rationale: Said State sovereignty over internal affairs is among his most deeply rooted convictions and urged warding off encroachments by the General Government.

state-harmful.rationale: Held that government must have the power to enforce its laws, that the Constitution secured liberty and property, and that the federal Union was the foundation of freedom.

strong-leader.rationale: Claimed broad executive powers (veto, removal of the Treasury secretary, Protest) but pledged to observe the limits of executive power and warned about executive encroachment.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Repeatedly recommended a constitutional amendment removing electoral colleges so the people elect the President directly.

indirect-election.rationale: Recommended removing all intermediate agency between the people and the election of President.

elective-rulers.rationale: Said the right of electing the Chief Magistrate belongs to the people and urged that office be conferred only through the majority's expression of will.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Recommended limiting the President to a single term of four or six years, though he himself sought and won a second term.

term-limits.rationale: Urged a single presidential term and rotation in federal office, but not limits for legislators; partial.

democracy-best.rationale: Held that the majority should govern and that the people, once informed, correct their own errors; stated trust in the people's ultimate judgment.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Said sovereignty is rightfully in the people's hands and that government must be administered for the good and will of the people.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Placed sovereignty in the hands of the people to whom every official is ultimately responsible, though he invoked Providence in speeches.

office-by-exam.rationale: Practised rotation in office with loyalist appointments, saying public duties are plain enough that intelligent men can readily qualify; no exam system.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Said long tenure in office breeds corruption and that officials turn government into an engine for the few at the expense of the many; denounced designing politicians in the Farewell.

corporate-influence.rationale: Farewell said moneyed corporations besiege legislatures and exercise more than their share of political influence.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Praised specific appropriation of public money by Congress and insisted Congress may tax only for its enumerated purposes.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Inferred: urged strict adherence to a written constitution of limited powers that secures liberty of conscience, the press and property.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Described his duty as commanding the forces and, in the Protest, claimed sole power to appoint and remove Cabinet officers.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Pledged to keep to the limits of executive power and said no individual, even a President, may disobey laws.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Farewell said a settled purpose of usurpation and oppression by government could justify an appeal to arms, though such cases were extreme.

political-violence-never.rationale: Said violence against the government is justified only in extreme cases; ordinary resistance is unlawful, and he used force against nullification (the Force Bill).

revolution-justified.rationale: Farewell allowed an appeal to arms only against settled usurpation and oppression.

right-to-secede.rationale: Nullification Proclamation: the Constitution forms a government, not a league; secession is not a constitutional right and is treason.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Used the threat of force and secured the Force Bill authorising the army to enforce the tariff against South Carolina.

minority-veto.rationale: Rejected a state's claim to nullify a federal law over a dissenting minority, calling it incompatible with a government.

natural-rulers.rationale: Said no one man has more intrinsic right to official station than another and that duties are simple enough for any intelligent citizen.

experts-over-public.rationale: Argued that public duties are plain and simple and that rotation in office is better than long experience; deferred to popular will.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Objected to artificial distinctions such as titles and exclusive privileges that make the rich richer.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Inferred: favoured election of the head of state by the people.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Said the military must be held subordinate to the civil power.

party-commands-army.rationale: Said the military must be subordinate to the civil power and that he would command the forces as President under the Constitution.

people-in-arms.rationale: Called the national militia the bulwark of defence and standing armies dangerous in peace, but still kept the army and navy.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Urged strengthening the navy, fortifications and militia, saying peace is best kept when it is understood the country is prepared for war.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Said each State has an unquestionable right to regulate its own internal concerns; opposed federal encroachment on their reserved powers.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Said States differ in their internal arrangements and that each State is the judge of its own concerns within the Union.

separated-powers.rationale: Held that Congress, the Executive and the Court must each be guided by its own constitutional judgment, and defended the executive in the Protest.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Built the Democratic Party and used appointments to reward party loyalists while President.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Called for a law banning abolitionist tracts from the Southern mails and condemned abolitionists, though he left other measures to the states.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Farewell: until a law is declared void by the courts or repealed, no one can justify forcibly resisting it.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Said unconstitutional or oppressive laws should be corrected through the courts or reasoned appeal, not resisted.

direct-action.rationale: Directed that remedies for bad laws be sought via the courts and free discussion, rejecting forcible resistance.

gradual-change.rationale: Closed the Bank veto in favour of compromise and gradual reform in the code of laws and political economy.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Stated that equality of talents, education or wealth cannot be produced by human institutions.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Said every man is equally entitled to protection by law, but owned slaves, signed removal and wanted abolitionist mail banned.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Tried to buy Texas from Mexico in 1829 and favoured its annexation; recognised Texas on his last full day in office (secondhand).

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Defended removal as a means by which Indians might share in the blessings of civilization under the paternal care of the General Government.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Rejected Cherokee independent government within states and said Indian claims to land they have not improved are visionary.

treaties-binding.rationale: Argued that treaties with Indians arose from necessity rather than principle and refused to treat tribes as independent nations; removal treaties were pressed on unwilling tribes.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Inferred: refused any independent tribal government inside Georgia and Alabama and required tribes to submit to state laws.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Held that tribes within states must submit to state laws and could be removed, so settlers' access to their land was not restricted.

population-transfer.rationale: Urged emigration west of the Mississippi and signed the Indian Removal Act; he called removal voluntary, but his administration pressed removal treaties, though it moved tribes within the country.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Bank veto said the Western states' debt to Eastern and foreign stockholders drained their currency to the East and abroad.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Contested: in 1835 he asked Congress to prohibit under severe penalties the circulation through the mails in the Southern States of incendiary publications intended to instigate the slaves to insurrection. This is a restriction on incendiary publications rather than hate speech as such.

empower-police-military.rationale: He asked for and signed the Force Bill of 1833 to enforce federal law, and in his first inaugural he calls the militia the bulwark of defence.

military-superiority.rationale: Inferred: he urged expanding the navy and forts and said the militia would render the country invincible, but he opposed a large standing army.

single-common-good.rationale: The first inaugural says the interests of agriculture, commerce and manufactures should be "equally favored", a balance of interests rather than a single common good reasoned out.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: As commander at New Orleans in 1815 he imposed martial law over the city's inhabitants because of doubts about their loyalty.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Inferred: the bank veto argues that a Supreme Court decision does not bind Congress and the president on the question of necessity, which limits judicial control of the elected branches. He did not speak of a majority as such.

notes:
Position changes: none material. Jackson favoured a bank 'wholly national' in early messages but vetoed the 1832 recharter. His 1829 recommendation of a single presidential term was not followed by his own conduct. Slavery, removal and the abolitionist mail question are scored from his messages and from record (reference source), with contested answers kept low.

Merged with an independent claude-haiku-5-5 audit: 6 answers taken from it, 33 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-haiku-5-5 notes: Positions are taken from his inaugurals, annual messages and vetoes, the 1832 Proclamation and the 1837 Farewell Address. The 1836 Specie Circular is known only from secondary summaries and maps to no statement. Several answers are inferred from his record on slavery and Indian removal and are marked low. Compilation page numbers were not recorded; the Richardson compilation PDF was searched by text.
